chapters.title: Chapter 3: Momentum Indicators - RSI, ROC, and Combining Signals

lessons.title: Case Study: Reading RSI Divergence on a Nifty Bank Stock

children.text: Lesson 2 promised a full case study on RSI divergence to close this chapter. Here it is, worked through on Bank of Baroda's run through the 2023-2024 PSU bank rally, the same broad rally introduced in Chapter 1's case study. The pattern is simple to state and easy to misuse: this lesson covers both the definition and the honest limitations of trading it.

body.text: Divergence occurs when price and RSI stop agreeing with each other. Bearish divergence is price making a higher high while RSI makes a lower high, a sign the rally is being driven by weaker underlying momentum than the last one. Bullish divergence is the mirror image on the downside: price making a lower low while RSI makes a higher low.

children.text: Divergence needs at least two comparable swing points to exist at all, it cannot be read off a single peak or trough. For bearish divergence: identify two recent price peaks where the second is higher than the first, then compare RSI's reading at each of those same two points. If RSI's second reading is lower than its first, despite price making a new high, that is bearish divergence, momentum weakening even as price extends. Bullish divergence mirrors this exactly on two troughs: a lower price low paired with a higher RSI low.
Case Study Setup: Bank of Baroda Through the PSU Rally

PSU banks, Bank of Baroda among them, were part of the broad new leadership group that drove the Nifty 50 to fresh highs through 2023 and into 2024, as covered in Chapter 1's case study. Take an illustrative run: Bank of Baroda rallies to a peak in December 2023, corrects, then rallies to a fresh, higher peak in May 2024. On the surface this looks like a continuation of the same strong trend. The RSI tells a more cautious story.

Bank of Baroda: illustrative 14-day RSI over the same period (approximate, rounded)

body.caption: Comparing the two peaks directly (illustrative figures)

body.text: This is a textbook bearish divergence: price at Peak 2 is clearly higher than Peak 1, but RSI at Peak 2 is clearly lower. The rally to a fresh high is being made with less underlying momentum behind it than the previous rally, a sign of a trend that is extending on borrowed strength rather than accelerating.

children.text: The divergence did not mark the exact top. Price pushed to one more marginal high in June 2024, around ₹270, even as RSI weakened further to 58, a deepening divergence rather than a resolved one. Only after that did the stock actually correct, falling to around ₹215 by September 2024, roughly a 20% decline from the June peak and about 17% below the price level where the original May 2024 divergence first appeared.

body.label: Decline from the divergence signal to the eventual correction low
body.context: From ₹260 in May 2024, where the divergence first confirmed, to ₹215 in September 2024, even though price still made one further marginal high in between

body.text: This is the single most important practical fact about divergence: it is an early warning about weakening momentum, not a precise timing signal for the top. Anyone who shorted the instant the May 2024 divergence appeared would have sat through a further move against them before being proven right. Anyone using it as a reason to trim a long position or tighten a stop would have been protected regardless of that extra month of upside.

children.text: How to Actually Use Divergence: Risk Reduction, Not a Standalone Signal

Treating a confirmed divergence as an automatic short entry ignores exactly the lag this case study just demonstrated. The more disciplined use, consistent with the combined-system thinking from Lesson 3, is as a risk-reduction trigger layered on top of an existing position: tighten a trailing stop, take partial profits, or simply stop adding to a long position, while still requiring an actual trend break, a death cross, or a close below a key moving average, before exiting entirely. Divergence tells you the quality of the trend is deteriorating. It does not, by itself, tell you exactly when the trend will actually end.

body.title: Spot the divergence
body.question: A stock makes a low of ₹100 in March, rallies, then falls to a new low of ₹90 in June. Its 14-day RSI was 25 at the March low and 34 at the June low. What does this show?
options: Bearish divergence, since price made a new low
Bullish divergence, since price made a lower low while RSI made a higher low
No divergence, since both price and RSI fell
This cannot be divergence because RSI never went below 30
body.explanation: Price made a lower low (100 to 90), but RSI made a higher low (25 to 34), the exact mirror image of the bearish case in this lesson. That combination is bullish divergence: selling pressure weakening even as price makes a fresh low.

body.title: Acting on the May 2024 signal
body.scenario: You are long Bank of Baroda from lower levels heading into May 2024. The bearish divergence in this case study confirms right as price hits ₹260.
body.prompt: Based on this lesson, what is a more disciplined response than immediately selling your entire position?
body.modelAnswer: A more disciplined response is to treat the divergence as a warning that momentum is weakening, not as a precise sell-everything signal. That could mean trimming part of the position to lock in some gains, tightening a trailing stop so a genuine reversal is captured without exiting on every day-to-day wiggle, or simply stopping further buying while still holding the core position until an actual trend break, such as a close below a key moving average, confirms the rally is genuinely over. This avoids exiting too early if price extends further, which it did here, while still respecting the early warning divergence provided.

body.label: Compare price and RSI swing highs visually on TradingView
body.description: TradingView's drawing tools make it straightforward to connect swing highs or lows on both the price chart and the RSI panel beneath it, the easiest way to spot a genuine divergence rather than trying to eyeball it from raw numbers.

cards.definition: Price makes a higher high while RSI makes a lower high, indicating a rally is losing underlying momentum even as price extends.
Price makes a lower low while RSI makes a higher low, indicating selling pressure is weakening even as price makes a fresh low.
A local peak or trough in price, the reference points divergence is measured between, requiring at least two comparable points to identify.

points: Bearish divergence is price making a higher high while RSI makes a lower high. Bullish divergence is the mirror image on the downside.
Identifying divergence requires at least two comparable swing points, never a single peak or trough on its own.

In this case study, Bank of Baroda's May 2024 divergence was real, RSI fell from 78 to 64 across two rising price peaks, but price still pushed to one further marginal high before the eventual correction.
Divergence is an early warning about the quality of a trend weakening, not a precise timing signal for exactly when a reversal will happen.

The disciplined use of divergence is as a risk-reduction trigger, tightening stops or trimming a position, layered on top of the trend and momentum tools from earlier in this chapter, not as a standalone entry or exit signal on its own.

This closes the chapter's toolkit: ROC and RSI for measuring momentum directly, moving average crossovers for trend context, combined systems for using them together, and divergence for reading when a trend's underlying strength is fading.
